stories.headline: Two fatal crashes in Denver early Sunday kill two, injure four
stories.summary:
Denver police investigated two fatal crashes early Sunday morning. The first, shortly after 12:30 a.m., involved two vehicles on southbound Interstate 25 near West Colfax Avenue, on the edge of the Lincoln Park and Auraria neighborhoods. Police said a man tried to pass another driver and collided with the front of the second vehicle, causing both cars to roll.

The man was thrown from his car and died at the scene. Three people in the passing vehicle and one person in the second car were hurt, and paramedics took four adults to the hospital. Part of the highway and two nearby on-ramps closed, and all closures had been lifted by 6:13 a.m.

About an hour later, at 1:21 a.m., police responded to a second fatal crash near South Sheridan Boulevard and West Evans Avenue in the Harvey Park neighborhood. A southbound driver struck a pedestrian who was crossing Sheridan mid-block, outside a crosswalk, and the pedestrian died at the scene. Sheridan reopened shortly before 6:30 a.m.

As of Sunday evening, no arrests had been made and both crashes remained under investigation. The Denver Office of the Medical Examiner will identify the two people who died.

stories.headline: Three members of New Castle family killed in Gunnison County plane crash
stories.summary:
Three people died when a small plane crashed Saturday morning in western Colorado's mountains, Gunnison County officials said. Emergency crews responded at about 9:20 a.m. to a remote wilderness area near Swampy Pass in the West Elk Wilderness of Gunnison National Forest.

All three occupants were found dead at the scene. Officials identified them as 46-year-old Mark Hendrickson, 15-year-old Alan Hendrickson and 13-year-old Case Hendrickson, all of New Castle in Garfield County.

The Gunnison County Sheriff's Office, the National Transportation Safety Board, the Federal Aviation Administration and the U.S. Forest Service are investigating the crash. The cause has not been released.

stories.headline: Election officials say ICE unlikely at Colorado polling places but are preparing
stories.summary:
Colorado election officials say it is unlikely that federal immigration officers will appear at polling places on Election Day, but some counties are preparing anyway. In Denver, which has gone to court to try to block ICE officers from voting locations, election workers are being trained to watch for immigration officers, document their presence and de-escalate any interactions.

Boulder County Clerk Molly Fitzpatrick is asking voters who see ICE officers at voting places to alert her office, or call 911 if they feel unsafe. Eagle County has folded the question into broader election worker training that covers emergencies, delays and weather problems.

About 90% of Colorado voters do not vote in person, since every registered voter receives a mail ballot. That means few voters would encounter officers even if they appeared.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said last month that ICE officers have authority to go to polling places if there is a threat or they are serving a warrant. The Department of Homeland Security said ICE is not planning operations targeting polling locations, though it left open arrests if there is an active public safety threat.

stories.headline: Ken Salazar joins opposition to Amendment 87 income tax measure
stories.summary:
Former U.S. Interior Secretary and Colorado Democrat Ken Salazar has joined Gov. Jared Polis in opposing Amendment 87, the graduated income tax measure on the Nov. 3 ballot. Salazar appears in English and Spanish broadcast and social media spots, filmed at a construction site, urging voters to vote no.

In the ad he says the measure would hurt workers and that Colorado needs to bring costs down. Salazar is a former state attorney general, U.S. senator and ambassador to Mexico.

Amendment 87 would replace Colorado's flat 4.4% income tax with a bracket system. Supporters say it would make higher earners pay a fairer share, with nominal cuts for the lowest brackets and a near doubling of taxes for the highest earners. Opponents estimate it would raise about $2.7 billion more per year.

The account comes from a Denver Gazette editorial opposing the measure, which reflects the newspaper's editorial position.

stories.headline: Polis declares disaster emergency for 12 counties as Four Corners flood waters recede
stories.summary:
Gov. Jared Polis declared a disaster emergency for 12 southern Colorado counties because of flooding. The declaration covers La Plata, Archuleta, Montezuma, Dolores, Hinsdale, San Miguel, Ouray, San Juan, Mineral, Alamosa, Rio Grande and Conejos counties. It activates the State Emergency Operations Plan and authorizes use of the Colorado National Guard.

Communities will get a break Monday as the storm system moves out, the National Weather Service in Pueblo said. Southern Colorado should dry out through Friday, though another strong storm is expected next weekend that may bring snow rather than rain.

In Archuleta County, closures included Wolf Creek Pass, parts of state highways 160, 151 and 17, and several county roads, with some expected to stay closed long term. The San Juan River in Montezuma County remained under a catastrophic flooding warning, and the National Guard hoisted a couple from a swept-away RV.

Once waters recede, officials will assess damage to determine whether to request federal assistance.

stories.headline: Colorado preschool providers frustrated by state help desk delays
stories.summary:
Childcare centers and school districts say long delays at the Colorado Department of Early Childhood have hurt their ability to take part in universal preschool. Gina Wallick, who runs Bee Curious Early Learning Center in Wellington, said she sent more than 50 emails seeking to register as a universal preschool site and received only automatic replies. She says the delay has cost her nearly $40,000 in state funding.

The department's help desk faced more than 900 tickets from parents, providers and districts over the summer. It has since cleared the backlog by adding staff and expanding office hours in August, and now responds in about a day.

The lapses have raised a larger question about which responsibilities belong to the state and which to providers and districts. Providers and districts want more control over enrollment so they can immediately make changes such as shifting a child from afternoon to morning sessions.

State officials argue enrollment belongs with the department so families can easily apply to multiple providers through a single system.

stories.headline: Broncos beat Cardinals 30-16; Waddle leaves with chest injury
stories.summary:
The Broncos beat the Arizona Cardinals 30-16 in Glendale on Sunday, but receiver Jaylen Waddle left the game with a chest injury. He was hurt with 4:51 left on a reverse play that lost 11 yards after a fumble, which Waddle recovered. Coach Sean Payton called the play dumb and awful after the game.

The severity of Waddle's injury was not known, and Payton gave no update. Waddle has 276 yards and a touchdown through seven games after the Broncos acquired him from Miami in March for a first-round pick and more. Defensive tackle Zach Allen left late with a right hamstring issue but said he would be fine.

Cornerback Pat Surtain II missed the game with an ankle injury. The Broncos host Kansas City next Sunday.

stories.headline: Rookie RB Jonah Coleman returns from injury, adds spark to Broncos offense
stories.summary:
Rookie running back Jonah Coleman returned Sunday after missing four games with an ankle injury, and had nine carries for 54 yards and two catches for 15 yards in the 30-16 win at Arizona. He was activated off injured reserve Saturday. Coach Sean Payton described what he brought as juice.

Coleman had two carries in the first half but ran seven times for 49 yards in the second half to help control the clock. The Broncos had 159 rushing yards after entering the game 26th in the NFL, though 62 came on a Bo Nix touchdown run.

J.K. Dobbins had six carries for 23 yards and a touchdown, and RJ Harvey caught a 52-yard touchdown pass. Payton said he wants to get Coleman more touches against Kansas City next Sunday.

stories.headline: Avalanche routed 6-2 by Predators in Nashville
stories.summary:
The Avalanche lost 6-2 to the Nashville Predators on Sunday night, their latest poor road performance. Nashville scored four power-play goals while Colorado's power play never came close to scoring, and the Avalanche have been short-handed 12 times over the last two games.

Former Avalanche players contributed. Ryan O'Reilly had four points, and Jack Drury and Ross Colton, both traded to Nashville over the summer, combined on a goal. Artturi Lehkonen scored his 10th goal and Jack Toews added one, while goalie Scott Wedgewood stopped 29 of 35 shots.

Rookie Fedor Svechkov sat out the entire third period. The Avalanche are 12 games into the season and have not shown a consistent effort level. They next face Connor Hellebuyck and the New Jersey Devils after a few days off.

stories.headline: Judge blocks Ridgway hotel from leasing rooms to Telluride-area construction workers
stories.summary:
A Ouray County judge sided with the town of Ridgway in a dispute over a hotel's plan to lease its 52 rooms to construction workers building a project in Telluride's Mountain Village. Judge D. Cory Jackson granted a preliminary injunction blocking the agreement between MTN Lodge's owner, Ridgway Suites LLC, and developer Merrimac Ventures.

Ridgway sued in March, arguing that long-term leases amount to household living in a zone that allows only lodging stays under 30 days. The owners said the hotel could not stay open without the contract, citing single-digit winter occupancy since they bought it in 2021.

The workers are building the $1 billion Four Seasons Resort and Residences. Jackson wrote that the town's interest in orderly land use outweighs any economic benefit, noting the hotel's argument that it need not pay lodging and sales taxes on stays over 30 days undermines its case. Surrounding communities have complained that housing burdens fall on them while benefits go to Mountain Village.

stories.headline: Aurora students quiz Colorado Supreme Court justices during Courts in the Community visit
stories.summary:
Members of the Colorado Supreme Court and the lawyers who argued before them answered questions from Aurora students Thursday at Overland High School. The visit marked the 40th anniversary of the Courts in the Community program, in which state appellate courts hear real cases outside downtown Denver each spring and fall.

Chief Justice Monica Márquez said that after joining the court she had to cut ties with lawyer friends to avoid conflicts of interest, which felt lonely. Justice Susan Blanco, who joined in March, discussed the judicial selection process. Márquez also presented challenge coins to participating teachers and staff for the first time.

Students in the Cherry Creek School District's criminal justice and law program received materials on the two cases about a month earlier. They read the briefs and held a moot court, and they reacted strongly to a case involving a senior living operator denied insurance benefits after COVID-19.
